The robbery collapsed inside sixty seconds. One moment Mr. Elm was following Mr. Ash through the service door of the diamond exchange, and the next the corridor was full of uniforms and shouting. Mr. Ash didn't hesitate. He put three rounds through the nearest officer, grabbed Elm by the collar, and dragged him back to the getaway car, shoving him into the passenger seat as glass spiderwebbed across the rear window. Tires screamed. They were clear.

Elm's hands were shaking. He thought of Pruitt, back in the safehouse, making him repeat the anecdote again and again—the invented drug bust in the public toilet, the invented arrest, the invented luck. "Tell it like you remember it," Pruitt had said, "because if you remember it, they'll remember it." And he had. He'd sat across from Bram and Cal and Mr. Ash and told the story so smoothly that Bram nodded and said, "Welcome to the crew, Mr. Elm," and just like that he was inside.

Now Mr. Ash was driving with one hand and reloading with the other, and Elm could hear sirens layering over sirens. They jumped a median. Ash cut down a side street, killed the lights, and for a breath the night went quiet.

They abandoned the car two blocks from the warehouse and ran. Elm's foot caught a curb and he went down hard. A woman in a parked hatchback saw them, fumbled for her keys, and Elm pulled her from the driver's seat. She had a small revolver in her coat pocket and she fired it blindly into his stomach. The pain was enormous, a white sound that swallowed everything. He shot her twice. She fell across the pavement and did not move.

Ash got him into a second car, drove the last few hundred yards, and half-carried him into the warehouse. He lowered Elm to the concrete and cradled his head. "You're not going to die," Ash said. "You hear me? You're not going to die."

Elm closed his eyes and thought of Ren Vasco walking out of prison that morning, stepping into grey light, reporting to Bram and Cal, who owed him for five years of silence. He thought of breakfast two days ago, the whole crew arguing about whether the song on the radio was about a girl or a drug, and whether the waitress deserved a tip. He thought of Bram handing out the tree aliases—Mr. Elm, Mr. Ash, Mr. Birch, Mr. Cedar—and Mr. Birch objecting, saying the name sounded like a coffin, and Bram telling him to take it or leave without knees.

Mr. Birch arrived at the warehouse alone. He looked at the blood, at Elm's grey face, and said the job had been a setup. There was an informer inside the crew. He took the bag of diamonds and hid them in a vent outside the building, then came back in and said nothing more about it.

Mr. Cedar strolled in twenty minutes later, humming. He opened the boot of his car and produced a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle, bound and gagged, and dumped him on the floor. Then everyone else left the room.

Left alone with the bound officer, Cedar turned up a radio oldie and danced to it, loose-limbed and grinning. He cut off Doyle's ear with a folding knife and doused him in petrol from a jerry can, still humming along to the chorus.

Elm shot him from the floor. The first round took Cedar in the chest and the second in the throat. Cedar sat down hard against the wall and died with his eyes open.

Elm looked at Doyle and said, "I'm a cop. The police are waiting outside for Bram. You understand? It's almost over."

Cal returned. He listened to Elm's account of what Cedar had done, looked at the body, looked at Doyle, and shot the patrolman dead himself.

Then Bram arrived. He stood in the doorway and said, "Mr. Elm is the informer."

Mr. Ash refused to believe it. He turned his gun on Bram. Cal turned his on Ash. The warehouse went very still.

All three fired. Bram dropped. Cal dropped. Ash fell beside Elm, still breathing, still gripping his weapon.

Elm looked up at the ceiling and said, "I'm a police officer. My name is Danny Roarke."

Ash stared at him. Then he shot him once in the chest, and the police stormed the warehouse, and Ash was cut down in the doorway, the radio still playing something old and gentle that no one was listening to.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett Rusk took control of the fortune and told the banker Barrow that of all his holdings, he wanted only the failing city newspaper, the Clarion. The ink was barely dry on the transfer papers before he moved into the building itself, sleeping on a cot in the back office, installing his manager Marsh at the ledger desk and his friend Devlin in the city room, and printing a signed statement of principles across the front page that promised the truth without fear or favor. Within a month he had hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and thrown a party that filled the street with a brass band and a chorus line, the whole city watching as Emmett Rusk announced himself.

Barrow had shaped the boy, after all. Years before, in a mining boarding house out west, Emmett's mother had signed her son over to the banker after a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich overnight. The boy had driven his sled into Barrow's stomach as the carriage waited, and been taken east away from his parents anyway, the sled left behind in the dust.

Returned from a buying trip abroad, Emmett arrived engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. The city approved. But a run of breakfast-table scenes charted the marriage cooling into silence behind separate newspapers held up like walls. Then Emmett met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat, and began visiting her rooms in secret, climbing the stairs with the careful step of a man who has found the one thing he cannot buy.

Mid-campaign for governor, the party boss Halloran brought Adele straight to Nora's rooms and threatened exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw. He lost the election. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city. The marriage collapsed like a mine shaft.

He married Nora and immediately forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Her debut was a humiliation that emptied the box seats of every friend he had left. A drunk Devlin began the savage review that Emmett finished himself, printed in his own paper, and fired Devlin for writing. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and Emmett finally let her stop.

He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall, the pieces scattered across a table built for forty. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel about nothing that was about everything, Nora packed and left him. He wrecked her bedroom, found a glass snow globe among the ruins, murmured "Bluebell," and carried it past the endless mirrors.

Alone at Silvermount, Emmett died with the word "Bluebell" on his lips and dropped the snow globe on the floor, where it rolled to rest against the baseboard.

A newsreel obituary recapped Emmett's public life in three minutes of flickering footage and closed without explaining his last word. The reporter Nash was sent to find out what "Bluebell" meant and was turned away by a drunk Nora in a seaside nightclub, her face ruined and hard. He read Barrow's memoir and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the butler Colm before concluding that no single word explains a life, as workmen shoveled a sled marked Bluebell into the furnace.

They met at a beach party at the end of the rail line, a seaside town where the tracks simply stopped. Tobias and Ivy wandered from the bonfire down the shore and found an empty house, its door unlocked, and broke in like children daring each other into a secret. The floor was sandy, the windows bare, and they sat with their backs against the wall and talked until dawn.

In a flat above a bookshop, a man and a woman sat on the floor with a tape recorder between them. Their own voices played back—sharp, cruel, relentless. She ran to the bathroom. She came back. Her eyes were red. She said, "So we try anyway." He nodded. They pressed stop.

Over two years they fell in love. He learned the topography of her: the ice on the frozen river where she slipped and he caught her elbow, the noodle house with the steamy windows, the drive-in where she fell asleep against his shoulder. Every season added a new room to the house they were building inside each other.

Rosa quit the clinic. She boxed the files, the session tapes, the intake forms, and mailed them to every patient on the books. She did not include a note. She included everything.

Then the relationship curdled. Recrimination over her drinking, his withholding, the way silence could fill a kitchen faster than smoke. She accused him of building walls. He accused her of flooding rooms.

They drove back to the city together. The highway lights streaked across the windshield. She said, "Come up." He followed her into the flat above the bookshop, and it was like walking into a house he'd never seen but somehow knew by heart.

Ivy came home drunk having dented his car. The fight was brief and total. She walked out and did not look back, and the door closed with the sound of something finishing.

Tobias skipped work. He could not say why. Something pulled at him like a tide he couldn't name. He took the train to the coast, stepped onto frozen sand, and saw her waiting there as if they'd agreed to this, though neither of them remembered agreeing.

Ivy hired a memory-erasure clinic. She signed the forms, submitted her mementos, and let the technicians map every trace of Tobias from her mind. When it was done, she felt lighter, she said. Like a room after you've taken the furniture out.

Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed. The flat felt strange. The pillow on the other side of the bed was undisturbed. He got up and made coffee for one and did not wonder why.

He visited the bookshop. Ivy treated him as a stranger. She was flirting with a young man behind the counter—Peck, his name tag said—and Tobias felt a jealousy he couldn't explain, directed at a woman he was sure he'd never met.

In the last surviving memory, the empty house on the shore. Tobias and Ivy stood in the bare room where they'd first talked through a night. She said goodbye. She told him to meet her at the beach. He reached for her and the walls dissolved.

Nina and Grady showed Tobias the form letter from the clinic, and he went to Dr. Hallam demanding the same procedure. He wanted what she had: the clean cut, the empty room.

Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure. Rosa kissed him. Then his wife appeared in the doorway holding a letter, a tape, a file. She said Rosa's own affair with Hallam had been erased. Rosa stared at the woman who had no memory of her and understood what she had done to others.

Tobias boxed up every object connected with Ivy. The scarf, the photograph, the chipped mug. He labeled each one so the clinic could map the memories attached. It was like packing for a trip he would never take.

Dell and Rosa got high on Tobias's bed. The machine hummed. The map on the screen drifted. They laughed about something unrelated and lost track of the procedure entirely.

The technicians Dell and Peck ran the overnight erasure in Tobias's flat. Peck pocketed the mementos when no one was looking. He planned to use them on Ivy, to see if anything still flickered behind those erased eyes.

Inside his own head, Tobias watched the memories he loved and changed his mind. He grabbed Ivy's hand and ran with her into memories she was never part of—hid her in the noodle house, in the drive-in, in rooms she'd never entered. But the walls kept dissolving.

He watched the most recent and ugliest memories dissolve around him one by one. The dented car. The slammed door. The silence. Each one went dark and he felt nothing, which was the point, and also the cost.

# Three Roads

## I. Ruben

The house had too many people in it. Ruben slept on a cot in the hallway, his mother in the back bedroom, and Nestor and Alma and the baby crammed into the front room with a blanket hung on a wire for a door. At night Ruben listened through it. Nestor came home smelling of adrenaline and cough syrup, money wadded in his fist, and when Alma asked where he'd been he hit her until the baby woke screaming. After that Ruben began to lean close to Alma in the kitchen, pressing his mouth to her ear. *Come with me. Just you and the baby. We'll go south.*

Nestor's dog Tigre was a rottweiler with a chest like a barrel. Ruben discovered what the dog could do when a neighbour's mutt slipped under the fence and Tigre tore it apart in the time it took to light a cigarette. He started bringing Tigre to the fights on Calle Madero, winning steadily, the dog's jaws dark with other dogs' blood. He paid two men from the fights to jump Nestor in an alley. Nestor came home with his face split open and his eyes changed. He took Alma, the baby, and the coffee tin where Ruben kept his winnings and vanished.

In the last fight the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring, claiming the dog had gone for him. Ruben pulled his knife and stabbed Chaco below the ribs and ran with Pipo into the night. He drove blind, running red lights at speed until he ploughed into a small car at the junction of Avenida Norte. The last thing he saw before the windshield came in was a woman's billboard face smiling down at him.

Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank two months later. At the funeral Alma stood by the grave with the baby on her hip. Ruben came to her in his only clean shirt. *Last chance,* he said. She looked through him and turned away.

## II. Celine

Hector left his wife and daughters on a Tuesday and moved Celine into a new flat that faced her own billboard. She could see it from the balcony — ten metres of her face selling perfume to the motorway. She stood there with her lapdog Chispa under her arm and felt the city looking back at her.

She woke in hospital with her leg pinned together, the bones held by a frame of steel and wire. No one could find Chispa. Hector had left the dog alone in the flat and it had fallen through a hole in the floorboards, into the cavity beneath. He tore up the floor, pulling up nails and splinters, but the dog had gone deeper, into the dark space between the joists where no hand could reach. Celine's leg turned gangrenous while he searched.

They amputated above the knee. The same week, the billboard came down. A crew in harnesses peeled her face from the sky and left the bare concrete.

## III. Cardo

Cardo was already at the junction when the cars met. He dragged the bleeding dog from the wreck, the rottweiler with the hole in its shoulder, and carried it away before the sirens started. He'd been a guerrilla once, then a vagrant, then a man who killed for money. The dog was one more broken thing.

He nursed Tigre back to health among his own pack of strays in a yard behind an abandoned warehouse. The businessman Elian found him there and offered cash to murder his half-brother Sergio. Cardo took the job but chained Sergio in the back room instead of killing him. He brought Elian face to face with his brother, set a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked out with money from both.

He watched his estranged wife buried from a hill above the cemetery. He followed his grown daughter Perla home and stood outside her flat in the rain. Tigre killed every dog in the yard while he was gone. Cardo came back to the bodies and put the gun to the dog's head and could not pull the trigger.

He broke into Perla's flat and left a long confession on her answering machine, his voice shaking, telling her everything. He took her photograph from the wall. Shaved and dressed in clean clothes, he left all his money in an envelope on her table and walked out into the wasteland with Tigre at his side.

The helicopters came first. All through the night they droned over the city, spraying for crop pests, their searchlights sweeping across rooftops and gardens, passing over every neighbourhood in the film that nobody was making yet but that the city seemed to be acting out anyway, each life a scene in something larger and stranger than itself.

Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess were getting ready for a dinner party. Bess was a painter. She stood before the mirror in a green dress while Neil knotted his tie and watched her reflection with the careful attention of a man memorising something.

Across town, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake. A boy called Charlie Rill. Otto wrote the name carefully in his book. He had no way of knowing the cake would never be collected.

Charlie was knocked down on his way to school by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona. She braked too late. Charlie stood up in the road, brushed himself off, and walked home insisting he was fine. He told his mother Elaine he felt sleepy. By afternoon he had collapsed into a coma, and his parents kept vigil at the hospital, the machines breathing for him, the room ticking.

Grant's estranged father Duff turned up at the hospital smelling of cigarettes and old rain. He sat in the corridor with Grant and confessed an affair from decades ago, a woman in a coastal town, a whole other life that had never stopped running parallel to this one. Grant listened and said nothing.

The cake went unbaked, then unbaked again. Unpaid and ignored, Otto Kemp began making anonymous phone calls to the family's house. He let the silence on the line do the work. Sometimes he breathed. Sometimes he said nothing at all and the nothing was worse.

Telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu sat beside her on the sofa, seething, the television muted, her voice low and professional and warm in a way it never was with him.

Stu and three friends drove out to fish. They found a young woman's body face down in the river, her hair fanned in the current. They tethered her to the bank with a rope and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. They drank beer and talked about the weather and did not look at the rope.

Vern's wife Iris, a party clown, was disgusted when she learned what the men had done. She sat at the kitchen table in her costume, the painted smile grotesque against her real mouth, and told Vern she would never speak to any of them again.

The singer Vida performed nightly in a club downtown while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home, practising scales in an empty house, the bow moving across the strings in the dark.

Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandoned the family dog in a parking lot to cover one of his lies. He told Peg the gate must have been left open. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and drove to her house with a handsaw and cut her furniture to pieces, the couch, the chairs, the bed frame, everything that had held a shape.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans and photographed Dot made up as a beaten corpse, lying on the bedroom floor, the bruises painted on with stage makeup, the camera clicking in the quiet house.

At the dinner party, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair. Neil made a scene. The guests watched their wine glasses. Nobody moved.

Charlie died in hospital. Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to confront Otto, who fed them warm bread and grieved with them, the three of them sitting in the back room among flour dust and the smell of yeast, eating in silence.

Bee found her mother asleep, closed the garage door, and killed herself with the car engine running. The cello sat in its case in the hallway.

At a picnic in the hills Stu smashed a young woman's head with a rock. The others were downstream. The river moved.

A tremor shook the entire city, and every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin, the anchor's voice steady, the helicopters still circling overhead.

The gun is in my mouth before I understand why. The metal tastes like blood and lye and everything Rex Marrow ever made me swallow. The trigger pulls. That's later. That's months from now, in a tower that's wired to blow. Right now I'm sitting in a church basement, crying.

I hadn't slept in four months. I'm a product-recall investigator — I track down defective chairs, cribs, toasters — and the insomnia turned everything to static. The only thing that worked was weeping. I started going to support groups. Brain parasites. Blood parasites. Bone marrow failure. I held hands with dying strangers and I wept and for a few hours after, I could sleep.

Then Ada Vey started showing up. She smoked during the testicular cancer meetings. She ate during the parasitic infection circle. Her faking was so obvious it broke whatever spell the rooms had on me, and the insomnia came back like a dog to its bowl.

On a business flight I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. He talked about fat and lye and the lies sold at department store cosmetics counters. I pocketed his card.

That night my flat blew up. Gas leak, they said. My catalogue furniture, my catalogue life — gone. I called Rex. He took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, the kind of place where the plumbing moans.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him. I did. He hit me back. We beat each other bloody in the car park and I felt something open up — not sleep, but something adjacent. We started doing it weekly. A basement. Rules: no shirts, no shoes, you go until one of you drops. More men came. Then more.

I'll be standing in a stairwell later, Rex's fist in my teeth, and I'll understand that the buildings are coming down. That's later. Right now the club is small and honest.

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her to the house and they started a loud affair I couldn't stand. The walls were thin. Meanwhile Rex was rendering fat he'd stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic, making soap, selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned my hand with lye one night and held me there, refusing to let me retreat into the meditation I used at the support groups. "Stay in the pain," he said. I stayed.

I blackmailed my employer. I used my own beaten face as evidence — pay me to stay away, or I'll tell them you knew. The cheques came every two weeks.

Rex turned the club into something he called Havoc. Shaven heads. Recruits who took orders. They vandalized corporate property, smashed glass, spray-painted slogans. The house filled with men who slept on the floor and answered to Rex.

Then Rex steered the car into oncoming traffic. He let it roll. When I woke up, he was gone.

A member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation. I started trying to shut it all down. But travelling city to city, I found identical clubs everywhere — men in basements, men who greeted me as Rex Marrow. I understood. He'd been building an army in his sleep. In my sleep. I worked it out: Rex was me. He'd been acting while I slept, walking out of the house in different clothes with a different voice, and I'd been losing the hours.

Ada confirmed it. She'd been sleeping with me, not with a separate man.

I discovered Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. I tried to defuse the charges. Rex beat me down a stairwell in one of the towers. I put the gun in my mouth — the gun, the metal, the taste I'd been tasting since the church basement — and I shot myself through the cheek to kill him.

Ada was delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. We held hands at the window. The buildings came down.

The hitmen's day began in the car, Rollo and Marcus driving across the city while debating foreign drug laws and what fast food was called abroad. They parked outside a flat and waited in the corridor, still arguing about whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for. When Marcus recited a passage of scripture, they kicked in the door and shot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, recovering a briefcase from the room. A fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them without hitting either, which Marcus called divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo's gun went off and blew the head off their passenger Del. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren's house, where a fixer directed the cleanup and gave the men fresh clothes.

Later, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. Marcus talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out.

Rollo bought heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up before his night out. He took Otis's wife Nadia to a themed diner where they won the dance contest. But Nadia snorted Rollo's heroin, overdosed, and had to be revived by an adrenaline shot to the heart on the dealer's living-room floor.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war had delivered to a young boy the gold watch his father kept hidden through years of captivity. The boy grew into the ageing boxer Denny. At Otis's bar, Otis paid Denny to take a dive in the fifth. Denny double-crossed Otis, won the fight and killed his opponent in the ring, then escaped in a taxi. Hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovered she had left his father's watch behind in his flat. He returned for the watch and shot Rollo dead with a submachine gun left on the kitchen counter. Denny and Otis collided in the street, crashed, and were taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny broke free, came back with a sword from the shop wall while one of their captors was raping Otis, and Otis declared them square on condition Denny leaves town. Denny collected Marielle and rode out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

Solly Two Coats had done it in the manner that would be talked about for years. He and his crew dressed as devout pilgrims, flowing robes and prayer beads and eyes cast humbly downward, and they walked into the diamond house in the northern port as though they had come to seek blessings. They walked out with a stone the size of a pigeon's egg. Within hours his cousin Marv, overseas, had sent word: bring it straight over, no stops, no fuss.

But Solly never was one to leave a city without turning a profit. Before he left, Grigor the Nail found him in a bar and told him about a bookmaker's in the city where the odds were generous and the doors were open to any man with cash. It was a kindness, Grigor said. Meanwhile, in a back room across town, Grigor was telling the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno exactly where Solly would be and when.

Boxing was the other business of the city. The promoters Halloway and Digby had a scheme that needed a fighter, so they sent Pretty Sam to a camp of travellers to buy a caravan for their operations. Sam was a big man, confident, but he was not prepared for the bare-knuckle fighter named Finn, who knocked him cold over the deal and left him in the mud. Now Halloway had no man for the fixed bout that the gang boss Coldstone had arranged. He had to put Finn in the fight instead and promised Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch, and headed for the bookmaker's to bet on the fight. Ike, Benno, and a man named Tulley were waiting. They bungled the robbery badly, taking Solly's arm and his case, but Grigor chased them off before they could finish the job. Solly stumbled away, bleeding, armless, and carrying nothing.

At the fight, Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune. He took it out on Halloway with his fists and worse.

Marv flew in and found Solly gone. He hired the bounty hunter Ledge, a thin man with a steady hand, to find him.

Grigor found Solly first. He cut off Solly's remaining arm to get the case open, and found that the stone was not inside it. The case was empty. Grigor stared at the stump and the blood and the nothing.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers. He shot their car to pieces on a back road and took both Ike and Benno along with the stone. But Coldstone had Solly by then, and Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs. He told Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong. They found Finn and told him to go down in the fourth, and Coldstone's men went to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan.

Grigor ambushed Ledge's car on the road with Ike and Benno still inside. The shootout was brief and final. Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. In the chaos, Tulley got away, and with him went a dog that had swallowed the diamond.

The second fight came. Finn knocked his opponent out again in the fourth round, and the travellers rose from the crowd with knives and guns and massacred Coldstone's men where they sat. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone in the aftermath and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished like smoke.

Weeks later, a dog was handed in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond on the floor, bright and perfect and covered in stomach slime. The pet shop owner called the number on the dog's tag, and by evening Halloway and Digby were standing in a room holding the stone that Solly Two Coats had carried out of the diamond house in the northern port, dressed as a pilgrim, with prayer beads in his hands and a lie on his lips. They looked at each other. They looked at the diamond. They had buried their partners and their fighters and their schemes, and now they held the thing that had started all of it, and neither one of them could think of a single thing to do with it.

He is in a hospital and another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer and the writer's stories are all about time and machines and the possibility of seeing what has not yet happened, which is of course impossible because everything has already happened. He comes home from somewhere and collapses. He is hospitalised. The walls are green and the food is green and the orderlies move through his room like figures in a diorama.

They are made to dig bodies out of the cellars. One of the diggers dies of the dry heaves. A fellow prisoner promises to have him killed one day on account of the scout. He says nothing. So it goes.

Emlyn stood in the hallway of Wilder's house with his coat still on and his hands in his pockets and said he had known for four years. He said Odile had told him on the trip abroad, standing in a hotel corridor with her shoes in her hand. He said he had never thought much of his friend's letters either. Wilder, who had telephoned him in a state not an hour before, could not find anything to say. The two men regarded each other in the half-light. Then Emlyn took his hands from his pockets and asked whether there was anything to drink.

The telephone call had come about because of a conversation in a bar. Two years had passed since the affair ended. Odile sat across from Wilder with a glass of something colourless and told him her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night confessing everything to Emlyn, every last detail, as though it were a matter she had simply forgotten to mention. Then she let slip, almost carelessly, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer Wilder represented—a writer the two men had always quietly detested, whose manuscripts they had once laughed over together. Wilder went home and sat with the telephone in his lap for a long time before dialling.

Before the bar, before the confession, there had been the evening Odile told him the marriage was finished. Before that evening there had been a longer stretch of ordinary life—two years of it—during which Wilder and Odile saw each other only at dinners hosted by the married couple, where Emlyn and Wilder discussed racquet games and schoolboy sport with such animation that Odile had no part in the talk at all. She would sit at the end of the table with her wine and listen to the two men carry on as though they were the ones bound to each other.

That stretch of ordinary life had begun when Wilder and Odile decided the rented rooms had become a chore. They split the crockery between them and surrendered the lease. She took the plates with the blue edges. He took the ones without. They carried the linen out in separate bags and did not embrace in the stairwell.

The rooms had lasted longer than they were meant to. After Odile told Wilder she was carrying her husband's child, the pair decided the rooms would go on exactly as before. She said it plainly, without tears, and he agreed plainly, and the next afternoon he brought flowers and they made tea in the kitchenette and the afternoon passed as the others had.

Before the pregnancy there had been a trip abroad. Odile and Emlyn stayed in a hotel in a city neither of them knew. At the desk Emlyn asked about a letter held for her, addressed in a hand he recognised. He turned it over once and gave it to her without comment. That evening she confessed. She told him about the rooms, the crockery, the afternoons. Emlyn listened and then remarked, as though it were a small disappointment, that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife. They did not speak about it again that night. When they returned home Odile went straight to the rented rooms and said nothing about the trip, and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had.

Emlyn had known, then, even before the lunch he took with Wilder at a restaurant with white tablecloths, where he drank steadily and baited his friend about contemporary fiction for two hours and never once mentioned what he had learned. Wilder had thought it a strange lunch. He had not understood it was a performance.

All of it had begun at a party at Emlyn's house. The guests were drinking downstairs. Wilder, who was Emlyn's closest friend, led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was. She did not leave the room.
